extracted.intended_audience: researchers in psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and music cognition (investigating music and social bonding)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and interpreting research on how music creates social bonds, emphasizing mechanisms (self-other merging and endogenous opioid/endorphin systems), appropriate experimental contexts, and measurement approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include both self-other merging and EOS (endorphins) mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of how music produces social bonding should consider both self-other merging due to interpersonal synchrony and neurohormonal mechanisms (the endogenous opioid system, particularly endorphins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues these two pathways have been investigated separately and that both are relevant; theories and empirical studies should not privilege only one mechanism (e.g., oxytocin alone) but examine interactions between motor/perceptual merging and EOS activation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ecologically valid group musical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Future experiments should recreate ecologically valid examples of musical activities involving groups rather than relying solely on dyadic laboratory tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs should reflect real-world group music-making (many participants, naturalistic movement and interaction) because dyadic studies give limited insight into large-scale musical activities; include group sizes and contexts typical of natural musical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer group contexts over dyads for assessing large-scale bonding
rubrics_metrics.description: Because musical activities historically and culturally involve groups, studies should examine social bonding in group settings rather than only dyads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dyadic synchrony is easily achieved and may overstate self-other merging effects; group contexts require rhythmic scaffolding and may reveal different mechanisms (e.g., EOS-mediated bonding) — so compare dyadic and group effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exertive (vigorous) movements to probe EOS/endorphin effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Exertive rhythmic activities (e.g., vigorous singing, dancing, drumming, rowing) are likely to release endorphins and should be used when investigating neurohormonal mechanisms of bonding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare high-energy musical engagement with low-energy or passive conditions; prior work (Dunbar et al., 2012b) shows vigorous active engagement elevates pain thresholds and positive affect more than passive listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish temporally coordinated movement from precise dyadic synchrony
rubrics_metrics.description: In large groups, rhythm provides an external predictable scaffold and bonding may arise from temporal coordination with music rather than identical simultaneous movements between individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate temporally coordinated behaviors and the role of rhythmic scaffolding; test 'synchrony with music' vs. direct inter-personal synchrony and consider measures of coordination that capture coordination to an external beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure EOS activation, using proxies when direct measures are infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Endorphin activity should be assessed when testing neurohormonal accounts; because direct assays are invasive/costly, pain threshold assays are an accepted proxy and neuroimaging (PET/fMRI) can show opioid-related activation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pain threshold tasks (ice water immersion, sustained squat, blood pressure cuff, electrocutaneous stimulator) as operationalized proxies; where possible, complement with PET/fMRI evidence of reward/opioid system activation and with behavioral/affective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include both active engagement and passive listening conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should investigate EOS and bonding effects arising from both active musical engagement (movement, singing, drumming) and passive listening, since both can engage motor regions and the EOS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare effects of active exertion (expected to strongly engage EOS) with passive listening (which also activates reward/opioid circuits) to determine relative contributions to social bonding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate and measure perception of agency/source of rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived source of rhythmic sound (agent-driven vs. inanimate) influences synchronization and bonding; experiments should manipulate and assess perceived agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include conditions where rhythms are produced by perceived human agents versus mechanical/drum sources (Kirschner & Tomasello, 2009; Launay et al., 2013, 2014); measure how belief about agency affects entrainment and social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use behavioral and self-report measures of social bonding
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess social closeness via multiple measures such as self-reported rapport, prosocial behaviors, cooperation, and physiological/affective indicators (e.g., mood, positive affect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine subjective reports (rapport scales), observable prosocial outcomes (cooperation tasks, generosity), and physiological proxies (pain threshold increases linked to EOS activation) to triangulate bonding effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and compare synchronized versus non-synchronized and exertive versus non-exertive conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental designs should systematically contrast synchronized/synchronous and non-synchronized conditions, and exertive and non-exertive activities, to isolate effects of rhythm, synchrony, and exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior findings show synchronized exertive activity elevates pain thresholds more than non-synchronized exertion; include factorial manipulations to dissociate synchrony, exertion, and music presence/absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for multiple neurochemical systems and their interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute bonding solely to a single neurohormone; consider oxytocin, dopamine, cortisol, cytokines, and growth hormones and their potential interactions with the EOS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies or interpretations that acknowledge contributions and interactions among neurochemicals (e.g., dopamine for reward, oxytocin for social processes, cortisol for stress), and be cautious about causal claims assigning effects to one system alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neural synchrony and phase-synchronization measures with interpretive caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Neural evidence (e.g., cortical phase synchronization, phi complex) can indicate shared involvement of networks during synchrony but does not by itself prove inter-agent neural merging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement neural synchrony metrics with behavioral and perceptual data; recognize that similar cortical networks across individuals may reflect making the same movements rather than true shared neural states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate and measure rhythmic predictability and tempo (dynamic attending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythmic predictability and tempo influence entrainment, arousal, and pleasure; studies should manipulate tempo and predictability as variables affecting bonding and EOS activation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply dynamic attending theory to test how predictability and tempo modulate emotional/motivational states and EOS-related responses (e.g., Huron, Husain et al., Margulis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate auditory-only synchrony and non-visual coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Synchronization and bonding can occur without visual access (auditory-only synchrony); experiments should examine synchronization when participants cannot see each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include conditions where participants synchronize via sound alone (Launay et al., 2014; Kokal et al., 2011) to separate visual mirroring effects from auditory entrainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multi-method approaches combining behavioral, hormonal, and neuroimaging data
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand mechanisms linking music to bonding, combine behavioral coordination measures, hormonal/proxy assays (endorphin proxies, cortisol), self-report, and neuroimaging evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-modal data allow testing whether self-other merging and EOS activation are linked or dissociable; use converging measures to strengthen causal inferences.
